stories.heading: The patients we walk beside.
stories.subtitle: Sickle Cell is not a statistic. It is a child missing school, a mother holding back fear, an elder who finally has a name for the pain. These are their journals.
stories.dignity: Shared with consent. Names changed where requested.
stories.contributeBody: If you or someone you love lives with sickle cell, your story can give courage to another family. Reach out to us — in Hindi or English — and we will listen.

meena.name: Meena
meena.alt: Portrait of Meena, a young Baiga girl from Dindori
meena.headline: "I want to finish school. The pain used to stop me. Now it doesn't."
body: Meena was nine when the pain in her bones first kept her home from school for weeks at a time. Her mother thought it was the cold; her grandmother thought it was the spirits.

When our screening camp came to Bajag, a single drop of blood gave her family an answer they had waited five years for. With monthly hydroxyurea and a simple folic acid routine, the crises that once filled her childhood have shrunk to a dull echo.
Today she is in Class 9, top of her Hindi class, and dreams of becoming a teacher in her own village so no Baiga girl loses years to a question no one could answer.

ramesh.name: Ramesh
ramesh.alt: Portrait of Ramesh, an elder Gond man from Mandla
ramesh.headline: "For fifty years I thought this pain was my karma. It was a disease."
body: Ramesh is fifty-two. He has worked the forests around Bichhiya since he was a boy. The joint pain came every winter, sometimes so severe he could not lift the axe.

He never knew the name for it. The block hospital had no test, the city was too far. When our camp arrived in 2023, his diagnosis came with both grief and relief — grief for the years lost, relief that his grandchildren could be tested early.
Both his grandchildren are now carriers, not patients. "My pain," he says, "will not be theirs."

savitri.name: Savitri
savitri.alt: Portrait of Savitri holding her young child
savitri.headline: "They told me my baby would not live. She is six now."
body: Savitri's first child was diagnosed with sickle cell at four months. The district hospital, kindly but exhausted, told her to be ready for the worst.
Through our care coordinator in Anuppur, she learnt the warning signs of a crisis, the importance of hydration, and the small daily medicines that change everything.
Her daughter is six. She runs, she draws, she fights with her brother over the last roti. Savitri now counsels other young mothers in her village — in Baigani, Hindi, and quiet, certain love.

arjun.name: Arjun
arjun.alt: Portrait of Arjun, a young schoolboy from Shahdol
arjun.headline: "My friend has the same as me. We are not alone anymore."
body: Arjun was screened at his school in Beohari at the age of seven. So was his classmate, Rohit. Both turned out to have sickle cell disease.
What could have been a heavy burden became a small, brave brotherhood. Their teacher learnt to spot the early signs of a crisis. Their parents joined the same WhatsApp group of carers.
Today, at nine, Arjun is the unofficial spokesperson of the school's monthly health circle — translating English pamphlets into the warmest, most matter-of-fact Hindi you've ever heard.

about.heading: Our Story, Our Promise
about.subtitle: Born from the belief that no family should fight sickle cell alone, we walk alongside tribal communities in Madhya Pradesh — bringing screening, care, and dignity to every village.

story.heading: How We Started
paragraphs: In 2023, a small team of health workers and community volunteers gathered in Anuppur with a simple question: why were so many tribal families living with undiagnosed sickle cell disease?

The answer led us deeper — into remote villages where healthcare was a day's journey away, where the pain was called 'karma' instead of a treatable condition, where children missed school and elders suffered in silence.

We started with one screening camp in Bajag. Then another in Bichhiya. Word spread through word-of-mouth, through ASHA workers who saw the difference early diagnosis made, through parents who finally had answers.

Today, Kiran Seva Sansthan works across six tribal districts of Madhya Pradesh — Anuppur, Dindori, Mandla, Shahdol, Umaria, and Sidhi. We have conducted over 240 camps, screened more than 50,000 individuals, and touched the lives of over 12,000 families.

But numbers don't tell the full story. What matters is the child who can now attend school without pain. The mother who knows how to protect her baby. The elder who finally understands that the pain was never their fault.

care.title: Compassionate Care
care.description: Free screening camps, treatment support, and follow-up care for every patient we serve. No one turned away. No family left behind.

awareness.title: Community Awareness
awareness.description: Education in local languages — Hindi, Baigani, and Gondi — so every family understands sickle cell, from symptoms to prevention to treatment options.

dignity.title: Dignity & Respect
dignity.description: We honor Baiga and Gond traditions, work with consent, and ensure every story is shared with dignity. Healthcare is not just medicine — it's humanity.

community.title: Community-Led Approach
community.description: We don't work for tribal communities — we work with them. Every camp is co-hosted with local ASHA workers, tribal leaders, and village health committees. The community knows what it needs; we bring the tools and support to make it happen.

transparency.title: Radical Transparency
transparency.description: Every rupee is accounted for. We publish impact metrics, maintain 80G tax compliance, and ensure donors see exactly how their contribution changes lives.

impact.title: Sustainable Impact
impact.description: We train local health workers, build relationships with district hospitals, and create systems that last beyond our presence. Real change doesn't end when we leave.

cta.heading: Be Part of the Change
cta.body: Whether you donate, volunteer, or simply share our story, you become part of a movement towards a sickle cell-free Madhya Pradesh. Every action counts.
